name: Backbone Rock Tunnel
dates: Year round, daylight; road closed in winter ice
unique: A railroad tunnel blasted through a seventy five foot knife edge of rock in 1901, still called the shortest tunnel in the world, with a staircase up the spine of the ridge and a creek running under the road.
buzz: Drivers duck even though there is room. The climb to the top of the rock is short and steep and gives a view straight down the tunnel mouth, and climbers use the face beside it.

name: The Snake US 421
dates: Year round, best spring to fall; ice in winter
unique: Four hundred eighty nine marked curves over three mountains and one valley between Mountain City and Holston Valley, a road motorcyclists ride from several states away and locals use to get to the store.
buzz: Riders rate it against the Dragon and say it is less policed and less crowded. The store at the north end sells the sticker, and everybody stops for the sign.

name: Shady Valley Cranberry Bogs
dates: Year round; best in October for the bog color
company: U.S. Natural Resources Conservation Service and private landowners
unique: A high mountain valley at 2,785 feet, the second highest community in Tennessee, where glacial relic cranberry bogs survived and have been restored as wetlands, with a driving loop, a boardwalk and a general store that sells cranberry everything.
buzz: Fall is the season and the bogs turn red. Birders come for the warblers and the valley is quiet enough that people mention the sound of the wind in the grass rather than any attraction.

name: Sycamore Shoals State Historic Park
unique: The ford on the Watauga where settlers wrote one of the first democratic documents in the American backcountry, where the Overmountain Men mustered in September 1780 before marching to Kings Mountain, and where a reconstructed fort and a museum interpret the Cherokee towns that were here first.
buzz: The fort and the muster story are the draw, and the staff fire muskets on program days. People are surprised to find a site this important in a town of fourteen thousand.

name: Liberty! The Saga of Sycamore Shoals
dates: Evenings in late June, several nights
company: Friends of Sycamore Shoals State Historic Area
unique: Tennessee's official outdoor drama, staged in the fort's amphitheater with a cast of local volunteers playing the settlers, the Cherokee and the Overmountain Men, ending with the muster that sent men over the mountains to Kings Mountain.
buzz: The volunteer cast is the charm, and the night the horses come through is the one people remember. Locals go every few years and take visitors.

name: Elizabethton Covered Bridge
unique: An 1882 wooden covered bridge over the Doe River, one of three historic covered bridges left in Tennessee and one of the few still standing in the middle of a downtown, with a small park and a sycamore shaded bank at each end.
buzz: It is the photograph everybody takes in Elizabethton, and the river below it is shallow enough in summer that children wade. The wooden interior smells like a barn.

name: Roan Mountain State Park
dates: Year round; road to the balds closed in winter
customer: Hikers, families, Appalachian Trail section hikers
unique: A park at the base of Roan Mountain with cabins along the Doe River and trails that climb from cove hardwood forest to the grassy balds on the state line, where the Appalachian Trail runs along the crest.
buzz: The balds are the reason people come and the climb is steady rather than technical. Cabins book months out and the river loops are where families with small children stay.

name: Roan Mountain Rhododendron Gardens
dates: Mid June peak bloom, festival third weekend of June
company: U.S. Forest Service and Roan Mountain Citizens Club
unique: The largest natural rhododendron garden in the world, on the shoulder of Roan High Bluff, where the Catawba rhododendron turns the slope purple for about two weeks each June and a festival has marked the bloom since the 1940s.
buzz: People plan a year ahead around the bloom and the parking lot fills by nine. When the timing is right it is the best flower display in the southern mountains, and when it is off the view is still worth the drive.

name: Nolichucky Gorge Rafting
dates: April to October, dam release dependent
company: USA Raft Adventure Resort and other licensed outfitters
customer: First time rafters, groups, families with teenagers
unique: A nine mile run through a steep gorge below the highest peak in the Unakas, with Class III and IV water, a railroad on one bank, the Appalachian Trail crossing overhead and no road in the bottom.
buzz: Outfitters call it one of the best whitewater runs in the Southeast and the guides point out the old railroad grade and the ospreys. Beginners finish tired and pleased.

name: USA Raft Adventure Resort
customer: Groups, bachelor parties, families, scout troops
unique: A river base camp with rafting, tubing, a ropes course and cabins, built on the banks of the Nolichucky where the gorge opens, so a group can stay two nights and be on the water both days.
buzz: Reviews praise the guides by name and the tubing in low water. Cabins are plain but the river is forty steps from the porch.

name: Unicoi County Apple Festival
customer: Families, craft shoppers, day trippers from Johnson City
unique: One of the largest street festivals in the region, filling downtown Erwin for two days with apple pies, cider, fried apple turnovers, hundreds of craft booths and continuous music on the courthouse stage.
buzz: The fried pies sell out and the crowd is measured in the tens of thousands. Locals say to arrive before ten to park, and that the cider is the reason to come at all.

name: Unicoi County Heritage Museum
customer: Local historians, railroad buffs, genealogy visitors
unique: A county collection in a 1903 frame house beside the Clinchfield Railroad grade, with the tools, photographs, furniture and schoolroom pieces of a mountain county that was built by timber, potatoes and the railroad.
buzz: Volunteers open it and walk you through, and the railroad material gets the most attention. The building itself, with its porches and pressed tin, is half the visit.

name: Vardy Community History Museum
company: Vardy Community Historical Society at the Vardy Presbyterian Church
unique: A museum in an 1899 Presbyterian church in a valley settled by Melungeon families, telling the story of a mixed ancestry community that was written about as a mystery for a century and has spent the last generation documenting its own genealogy and defending its own name.
buzz: Visitors come expecting folklore and get records, photographs and family trees. Descendants run the place and answer questions about the racial categories that were used against their grandparents.

name: Mahala Mullins Cabin
unique: The cabin of Mahala Mullins, the Melungeon woman said to have weighed four hundred fifty pounds and to have sold moonshine through a window because she could not be carried out of the house to be arrested, a story retold in local histories and on the state historical marker.
buzz: It is a small log cabin beside the church and the story travels further than the building. Visitors say the marker is worth reading twice and the setting is prettier than they expected.

name: Hancock County Museum
company: Hancock County Historical and Genealogical Society
unique: A county historical society museum in the old jail, holding the photographs, ledgers, quilts and family files of one of the poorest and most remote counties in Tennessee, where the Clinch River and the mountain ridges kept the place to itself for a century.
buzz: The genealogy files are the real collection and volunteers will pull a family folder for you. Call first, because the hours depend on who is available.

name: Clinch River at Kyles Ford
unique: A float through the Clinch River's mussel beds, one of the most biologically diverse stretches of river in North America, with a canoe launch at Kyles Ford and muskrats, herons and the occasional hellbender under the ledges.
buzz: Anglers float it for smallmouth and paddlers for the quiet, and both mention the water clarity. Shuttle service is limited, so most people run two cars.

name: Historic Rogersville
unique: One of the oldest towns in Tennessee, laid out around a spring in the 1770s, with a National Register district of brick and frame storefronts, a 1830s Presbyterian church and a courthouse on the hill where the lost State of Franklin and the first years of Tennessee politics were argued.
buzz: It is the kind of small downtown that people photograph and then say they had never heard of. The antique shops and the inn are the reason to stay the night.

name: Hale Springs Inn
unique: A three story brick inn that has put up travellers since the 1820s, restored with period furniture and a dining room that serves mountain trout and cornbread in a town where three presidents and a long list of circuit judges once ate.
buzz: Guests mention the floors, the porches and the quiet more than the food, and locals book the dining room for anniversaries. It is the only place to stay downtown.

name: Ebbing and Flowing Spring
unique: A spring that rises and falls on a regular cycle, one of only two of its kind known in the world, in a hollow a few minutes from Rogersville where the water gathers and then drains away on its own schedule.
buzz: People stand and wait for it to ebb, then wait again for it to come back. It is a fifteen minute stop that people talk about for years because nothing about it looks mechanical and it will not hold still.

name: Amis Mill and Falls
dates: Grounds year round, mill on event days
unique: The stone mill, dam and falls built by Thomas Amis in the 1780s on Big Creek, one of the first industrial sites in the Tennessee country, where the millrace, the millstones and the stone house still stand in a wooded hollow.
buzz: The falls and the stone work are the draw and the place is nearly empty. Photographers come after rain when the water is up.

name: Pressmen's Home
dates: Exterior year round, respect private property
company: Private owners, historic district listed on the National Register
unique: A whole town built in a Poor Valley hollow by the International Printing Pressmen's Union, with a trade school, a sanitarium, a hotel, a farm and a swimming pool, abandoned since the union left in 1967 and still standing in the trees.
buzz: Photographers and labor history people make the drive. Most of the buildings are unsafe and privately owned, so the visit is from the road, and the scale of the place in the middle of nowhere is what people describe.

name: Grainger County Tomato Festival
dates: Third weekend of July, Friday and Saturday
customer: Families, tomato growers, day trippers from Knoxville
unique: A festival built on the county's reputation for tomatoes grown in Clinch Mountain soil, with nearly a hundred forty vendors, tomato sandwiches, a tomato tasting, a quilt show, a 5K and a Friday night opry of local talent.
buzz: People drive from Knoxville for the tomato sandwiches and the fried green tomatoes. It is crowded, hot and worth it, and the local growers sell out by mid afternoon.

name: Grainger County Quilt Trail
unique: Painted wooden quilt squares mounted on barns, sheds and storefronts across the county, each one a real quilt pattern chosen by the family that owns the building, mapped into a driving route over Clinch Mountain.
buzz: It is a scavenger hunt with no entry fee. People photograph all of them over a weekend, and the barn owners often come out to explain the pattern.

name: Cherokee Lake at Bean Station
dates: Year round, best May to October
unique: A TVA reservoir with more than four hundred miles of shoreline in the Holston valley, where the drowned town of Bean Station sits under the water and the coves above it hold bass, crappie and the marinas that serve them.
buzz: Anglers rate it among the best bass lakes in east Tennessee and the coves are quiet on weekdays. Locals remember the town that went under when the dam came.

name: Panther Creek State Park
unique: Fourteen hundred acres on the Cherokee Reservoir with seventeen trails and more than thirty miles of them, ridgeline views over the lake and a swimming beach, built on land the Depression era park crews shaped.
buzz: Locals treat it as the backyard and the trail system is bigger than people expect for a county park. Sunset from the Point is the standard recommendation.

name: Rose Center
company: Rose Center Council for the Arts
unique: An 1892 school building converted into a community arts center, with galleries in the old classrooms, a theater in the auditorium and studios where local potters, painters and quilters teach.
buzz: It is the cultural living room of Morristown and the galleries are free. People mention the woodwork and the staircase as much as the exhibitions.

name: Downtown Morristown Farmers Market
unique: A Saturday market on the square where growers from Hamblen and the surrounding mountain counties sell tomatoes, beans, sorghum, apples and baked goods, with the courthouse and the 1890s storefronts as the backdrop.
buzz: Small, early and genuine, with the same growers every week. People come for the tomatoes and stay to talk, and the market is a good reason to walk the rest of downtown.

name: Andrew Johnson National Historic Site
unique: Three pieces of a life within a few blocks: the tailor shop where Johnson worked, the early home, and the later brick house, plus the cemetery on the hill where he is buried under a flag he insisted on being wrapped in, the only president to do so.
buzz: Rangers give the best version, and the tailor shop is the part that surprises people, a working man's trade preserved inside a national site. The cemetery walk uphill is short and worth it.

name: Greeneville Historic District
unique: A downtown of brick storefronts and antebellum houses around a spring fed square, in the town that was the capital of the short lived State of Franklin and later a Unionist island in east Tennessee.
buzz: The square and the side streets are compact enough to walk in an hour and the shops are local. People pair it with the Andrew Johnson site and lunch.

name: Doak House Museum
customer: History buffs, architecture fans, school groups
unique: The 1830 home of Samuel Witherspoon Doak, the Presbyterian minister who founded Tusculum College and taught a generation of frontier preachers, with the original floors, the meeting room and a garden of heirloom plants.
buzz: It is run by the university and the tours are given by people who know the family. Small, quiet and a good counterweight to the political history downtown.
